title: twr box add
description: Add a box the hub reaches over SSH, or through a command (--command: a container): no token, listener or tunnel. Probes the box with ssh in this terminal (ssh may ask about its host key or for a passphrase), checks that ssh also works without prompting (the hub's never prompts), says what will happen and asks y/N (without a terminal, only with --yes). A command is probed as the hub runs it: without a terminal, so nothing it runs may prompt, and checked to pass the hub's input to the box (`-i`) without giving it a terminal (no `-t`). Then writes `[boxes.<name>]` to boxes.toml, next to config.toml, and adds the box to the running hub (starting one when none runs). The hub installs its own twr build on the box (same OS and CPU; else run `twr box install <name>`), connects and starts a twr box daemon there, which runs the box's threads. Waits up to 90 s for the box to come online. Boxes belong to the default workspace.

fields.label: name
fields.description: The box's name: letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-` (not starting with `.` or `-`; not `local`)

fields.label: ssh
fields.description: The ssh destination (`me@host`, or a host from `~/.ssh/config`), with any ssh options before it (`-p 2222 me@host`): one argument or several words, joined with spaces. With --command, the command the hub runs to reach the box (`docker exec -i <container>`), its words passed as they are, not through a shell. None with --dial-in

fields.label: dial in
fields.description: A dial-in box: its runner connects to the hub (`twr runner install-token` on the box). Given before any other word, with --hub

fields.label: hub
fields.description: With --dial-in: the URL the box's runner dials to reach this hub's listener: `wss://` (Tailscale serve, or `[hub] tls`), or `ws://` to a loopback address (an ssh tunnel's end on the box)

fields.label: ca
fields.description: With --dial-in and a wss:// URL: the CA certificate (PEM) the box's runner trusts, by its absolute path on the box

fields.label: command
fields.description: The words are the command the hub runs to reach the box (`docker exec -i <container>`, `kubectl exec -i -n <ns> <pod> --`), with `sh -c <what ssh would run>` appended, instead of an ssh destination. Given before the words. For `docker`, `podman` and `nerdctl exec -i` and `kubectl exec -i`, the same command with `-t` becomes its terminal_command (for `twr box login` and `twr box project --clone`)

title: twr box doctor
description: Check a box and say how to fix what is wrong: the hub's view of it (when a hub runs), ssh without prompting (as the hub runs it) and in this terminal (a command box: its command, and that it passes the hub's input without a terminal), the box's OS, CPU, data directory and twr builds, its box daemon, logind (Linux), its agent CLIs (path, version, login), git, free disk, and the projects configured for it. Works without a hub and with the box offline. The checks on the box run the hub's twr build when it is there, else the box's configured build, else the newest one there, and say which. Never shows account details. Exits 1 when a check failed (✗)

fields.label: name
fields.description: The box's name

fields.label: json
fields.description: Print the checks as JSON

title: twr box install
description: Install twr on a box the hub connects to (ssh or command) and have the hub connect to it again. On a box of the hub's OS and CPU the hub installs its own build. On another one: with --binary, that file; with --from-box, a twr already on the box (built there with docs/tools/dev-install.sh, say); otherwise, when the hub runs a release, the release's archive for the box (its signed checksums verified as `twr update` verifies them), unpacked on the box. The build is recorded as the box's `build` in boxes.toml (a box of config.toml: the line to add is printed). Asks y/N before installing (without a terminal, only with --yes). Waits up to 90 s for the box to come online; a box online on another build is switched once it has been quiet for 2 minutes, and that is waited for too (at most about an hour and a half, printing the box's notes meanwhile; about two hours when its daemon speaks an older runner protocol that the hub drains first, letting its running turns finish)

fields.label: name
fields.description: The box's name

fields.label: binary
fields.description: A twr executable built for the box's OS and CPU, to upload instead of a release's

fields.label: from box

Then says whether the agent is logged in (the box daemon's view through the hub when one runs, else the box's). Needs a terminal

title: twr box project
description: Find a project's repository on a box, or clone it there, and record where it is (`[boxes.<box>.projects.<project>] repo`, in boxes.toml), so that `twr thread new <project> --box <box>` uses it. The project is a configured one, or a repository folder name under project_roots, as `twr thread new` finds it on this machine. Without options, the box's twr build (as `twr box doctor` picks it) looks at the path the repository has under your home here, under the box's home, then under the box's ~/code, ~/src, ... for a repository of that folder name, and reads each one's origin. When exactly one has the project's origin and the search was complete, it asks y/N (--yes: it doesn't) and records it; otherwise it lists them, and --path picks one. --path records the repository there once the box says it is one (its top level). --clone runs `git clone` of the project's origin on the box, in this terminal, with the box's own git credentials (no agent forwarding), then records the clone; it needs a terminal (and on a command box, its terminal_command). twr never fetches. A running hub takes the change at once

title: twr box restart
description: Restart the daemon of a box the hub connects to (ssh or command): the hub ends its connection to the box and connects again, having the box stop its daemon (and the agents it runs) and start a new one. On a Mac, after someone logged in at its screen, the new daemon runs in that GUI session, where Claude Code can read its keychain login. Asks y/N first (without a terminal, only with --yes), then waits for the box to come back online (as long as the hub's attempts may take: an hour and twenty minutes at most, when the old daemon has a repository change to finish and a build to upload, printing the box's notes meanwhile) and says how its daemon was started. While the hub drains the box (its daemon speaks an older runner protocol), the restart stops its agents cleanly first, as the drain would: no crash

description: Start an implementation loop in a thread: it plans the task, has the plan reviewed when it touches a contract, implements it with the gates green, then runs the review loop on the result, and commits at the end. Changes already in the worktree are the loop's baseline: out of its scope and out of its commit. It starts at once on your saved loop settings; the first time, with --setup, or when a saved setting no longer holds, the thread's settings card comes first, as for `twr loop review`, with one more answer when it holds a task: run without a loop (the task goes to the thread as your own message). Without a terminal the card stays open, this prints the `twr respond` lines for it, and exits 2

title: twr model
description: Show or set a thread's runtime, model and reasoning effort. With only the thread, shows them. The model is the runtime's own id or alias (Claude Code: `fable`, `opus`, `sonnet`, or a full id such as `claude-fable-5-2`); `default` returns the model or the effort to the runtime's default (once the thread has a session, only where a resumed session takes it: Claude Code's effort; the hub refuses the rest, except with `--runtime`). A running runtime finishes its turn first, then restarts on the same session with them; an idle one restarts now; a parked or stopped one starts with them next time. With `--runtime`, the thread moves to that runtime: its current runtime stops (after the turn it runs), and its next turn starts a new session of the new one, given a handoff of what the previous session did; a model or effort left out is the new runtime's default. Moving back to a runtime it left a session of resumes that session instead, told what the thread did since, with the settings it had (`default` starts a new one). Not for the orchestrator (switch it with `twr orchestrator use`); a pty thread can only move to another runtime
